issues.legal_issue: A tenancy of an open plot on which the tenant has put up a shed does not make the plot premises under the rent-control law, and possession may be recovered through a civil suit.
material_facts: The allotment records and the tenant society’s earlier representations described the allotted property as a plot or open compound and indicated that the society had constructed the shed.
The evidence supported the finding that the tenancy was of the plot, rather than of a building.
The landlord brought a civil suit for possession after terminating the tenancy.
The courts below concurrently found that the property allotted to the society was only a plot of land.
issues.conclusion: The property let to the society was only a plot of land, not premises under the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958; the landlord was entitled to seek possession by a suit in the civil court.
issues.legal_principle: The nature of the tenancy is determined from the property actually allotted and let, assessed on the evidence. References to “industrial premises” in a general, cyclostyled allotment form did not establish that a building was let. The Court did not decide whether a plot with a shed would qualify as premises in the abstract. It referred to section 2(i) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958, and to Corporation of City of Victoria v. Bishop of Vancouver Island, Karnania Properties Ltd. v. Augustin, State of Bombay v. Sardar VenkatRao Krishna Rao Gujar, Ghanshiam Das v. Devi Prasad, Uttam Chand v. S.M. Lalwani, S.M. Gopalkrishna Chetty v. Ganeshan, and Morarji Goculdas Deoji Trust v. Mahadev Vithan Kutwa, but found it unnecessary to decide the broader plot-and-shed question in light of its conclusion on the facts.

rule.if: civil_suit_for_possession and tenancy_of_open_plot and tenant_constructed_shed and records_support_plot_allotment

predicates.civil_suit_for_possession: A landlord brings a civil suit seeking possession of property occupied by a tenant.
predicates.tenancy_of_open_plot: The tenancy granted to the occupant is of open land rather than a building.
predicates.tenant_constructed_shed: The occupant constructed a shed on the land after it was allotted or let.
predicates.records_support_plot_allotment: Contemporaneous records and the occupant’s earlier representations support that only the plot was allotted.

issues.definition: When a landlord seeks possession in a civil suit and the tenancy was of an open plot, the occupant constructed the shed, and the records support that only the plot was allotted, the civil possession suit is maintainable.

issues.legal_issue: A tenant cannot take a position contrary to a final finding between the same parties in an earlier rent-control proceeding when principles analogous to res judicata apply.
material_facts: The society applied under section 44 of the Delhi Rent Control Act for permission to make repairs.
The Rent Controller found that the society was tenant only of an open site and that the shed had been constructed by the society.
That finding became final between the parties.
In the later possession proceedings, the society sought to contend that the property was premises covered by the Act.
issues.conclusion: The society could not take a contrary position in the later proceedings because the Rent Controller’s finding had attained finality between the parties and principles analogous to res judicata applied.
issues.legal_principle: A final finding between the same parties may, on principles analogous to res judicata, prevent a party from taking a contrary position in later proceedings. The Court applied that principle to the Rent Controller’s finding in the society’s application under section 44 of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958.

rule.if: later_proceeding_between_same_parties and earlier_rent_control_finding and earlier_finding_became_final and party_takes_contrary_position

predicates.later_proceeding_between_same_parties: A later proceeding is brought between parties who were also parties to an earlier proceeding.
predicates.earlier_rent_control_finding: A rent-control adjudicator made a finding about the nature of the tenancy in an earlier proceeding.
predicates.earlier_finding_became_final: The earlier finding became final between the parties.
predicates.party_takes_contrary_position: A party in the later proceeding advances a position inconsistent with the earlier finding.

issues.definition: If the same parties have a later proceeding after a final rent-control finding and a party advances an inconsistent position, that contrary position is barred.

issues.legal_issue: The Supreme Court does not normally reappraise evidence or interfere under its special appellate jurisdiction with concurrent findings of fact.
material_facts: The Assistant District Judge, Additional District Judge, and High Court all found that the society had been allotted only a plot of land.
The appeal challenged those concurrent findings.
The Supreme Court reviewed the evidence and found no basis to reach a contrary conclusion.
issues.conclusion: The Court did not interfere with the concurrent findings of fact and dismissed the appeal.
issues.legal_principle: Under Article 136 of the Constitution, the Supreme Court does not normally reappraise evidence or interfere with concurrent findings of fact, even where another conclusion might be possible on the evidence.

predicates.appeal_from_concurrent_fact_findings: An appeal asks the Supreme Court to disturb factual findings that the lower courts reached concurrently.
predicates.findings_supported_by_evidence: The concurrent findings have evidentiary support in the record.

issues.definition: When an appeal challenges concurrent factual findings that are supported by evidence, the Court normally does not interfere with those findings.
